query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small, controlled amount of Ti to equiatomic NbMoTaW will improve its room-temperature ductility by enhancing grain boundary cohesion without compromising its high-temperature strength or irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase equiatomic NbMoTaW, which exhibits excellent high-temperature (1600 °C) mechanical properties and predicted irradiation resistance but very poor room-temperature ductility.
generation.intervention: Introduce trace levels of Ti (e.g., up to a few atomic percent) uniformly into the NbMoTaW alloy.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature testing for ductility; high-temperature (1600 °C) mechanical testing; and controlled irradiation experiments (e.g., ion irradiation) to assess radiation resistance.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced grain boundary cohesion, potentially via Ti segregation at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Ti atoms preferentially segregate to grain boundaries, strengthening intergranular cohesion and limiting brittle intergranular fracture at room temperature. Since Ti is a refractory element, it is expected to integrate well into the NbMoTaW matrix, thereby not significantly altering high-temperature deformation mechanisms or compromising defect migration barriers that underpin irradiation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: At room temperature, the Ti-doped alloy will exhibit improved ductility (e.g., higher plastic strain or elongation). At 1600 °C, the yield strength and overall mechanical performance will remain similar to the untreated alloy, and the irradiation resistance will not be adversely affected.
generation.baseline: Untreated, single-phase equiatomic NbMoTaW alloy with known excellent high-temperature properties and predicted irradiation resistance but limited room-temperature ductility.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only for trace Ti additions that do not exceed a threshold where secondary phases or detrimental microstructural evolution occur. Excessive Ti could potentially form unwanted phases that might negatively impact high-temperature or irradiation properties.
generation.uncertainty: While literature suggests Ti can enhance ductility through improved grain boundary cohesion, the optimal Ti concentration and the quantitative gains in ductility without any trade-offs in high-temperature performance and irradiation resistance require experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of NbMoTaW alloys with systematically varied, low-level Ti additions (e.g., 0%, 0.5%, 1%, and 2% atomic Ti). Perform comprehensive mechanical testing at room temperature (tensile and/or compressive ductility measurements), high-temperature mechanical tests at 1600 °C, and controlled irradiation experiments (using ion irradiation to simulate radiation damage). Additionally, use microscopy (TEM/SEM) to assess grain boundary structure and check for secondary phase formation.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile or compressive ductility (percent elongation/plastic strain)
High-temperature (1600 °C) yield strength and mechanical performance parameters
Irradiation response metrics (defect density, microstructural evolution under irradiation)
Grain boundary analysis for signs of improved cohesion and absence/presence of secondary phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if (a) Ti additions do not result in a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility compared to the baseline, (b) if high-temperature performance or irradiation resistance is measurably degraded relative to the untreated NbMoTaW, or (c) if detrimental secondary phases appear as a result of the Ti addition.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years []. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co []. First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [,]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 []. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [] and yield strength σ0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa [].
